title: User Execution
summary: User Execution describes adversary reliance on a person to take an action that results in code running or a security decision being made in the attacker interest. It is the human step that completes many delivery chains: opening an attachment, enabling macros or add-ins, clicking through a security warning, running a downloaded installer, mounting a disk image, pasting and executing a copied command, or approving a fraudulent push notification. The technique appears wherever an adversary cannot reach a system directly and must borrow a legitimate user session and its privileges, which makes it relevant on Windows, macOS, Linux, mobile platforms and cloud consoles alike. The artefacts are a mixture of endpoint and identity telemetry: process creation showing a document reader, archive tool or installer spawning a shell or a scripting host, file creation in download and temporary directories, mark-of-the-web and quarantine attributes, macro and add-in events in productivity suites, click-through records for protected-view prompts, and authentication logs for push-notification or help-desk style social engineering. Investigators distinguish malicious from benign execution by examining the parent process, the file origin and zone information, whether the resulting process made outbound network connections, whether the same lure reached other users, and whether the account later exhibited behaviour inconsistent with its history. Because the triggering action is legitimate and user-driven, prevention leans on policy and interface friction rather than detection alone, and the honest measure of a control is how many prompts an ordinary employee must evaluate during a normal working day before the prompts themselves become the vulnerability.
objectives: Explain how user-initiated execution differs from remote exploitation and why that shapes the defensive response.
Trace a document, archive or installer parent process to the child processes and network activity it produced.
Read mark-of-the-web, quarantine and macro telemetry to establish how a file was obtained and opened.
Evaluate user-facing controls such as attachment policy, macro restriction and prompt design against real user behaviour.
Write detection logic for productivity and reader applications that spawn interpreters or shells.
Rank response urgency when a user action is confirmed versus merely suspected.
